newsitem.title: USA: Jury selection proceeds in Florida's Broin case.
newsitem.headline: Jury selection proceeds in Florida's Broin case.

text.p: Eight more potential jurors were selected for a landmark class-action lawsuit filed against tobacco companies on behalf of flight attendants -- a case that attorneys said would go ahead in spite of Friday's sweeping accord between U.S. states and the tobacco industry.

The potential jurors added Monday, the 13th day of jury selection, brought to 83 the number in the pool from which attorneys will select a panel of six jurors and an estimated 10 alternates for the case, known as Norma Broin vs. Philip Morris Cos Inc, et al.
Eventually, the pool is expected to include 100 people.

The suit was filed on behalf of thousands of flight attendants allegedly sickened by breathing secondhand cigarette smoke on U.S.-based passenger jets. It is the first class action and first secondhand smoke case against tobacco companies to make it to trial.

Presiding Judge Robert Kaye told the court he expected the case to go ahead in spite of a $368.5 billion settlement agreement announced between state attorneys general and major tobacco firms. The accord provides the industry with some immunity from litigation, including future class-action suits.

Attorneys involved in the case said the same, although lawyers for Philip Morris and R.J. Reynolds Tobacco Co were traveling to New York to determine how, if at all, the proposed settlement would affect the Broin case.
"Judge Kaye indicated very strongly today that he's going forward," said Stanley Rosenblatt, an attorney for the plaintiffs.

Separately, an emergency hearing in another class-action suit, Engle vs. R.J. Reynolds -- also filed by Rosenblatt and his wife and co-counsel, Susan Rosenblatt -- was postponed from Monday at 1730 EDT (2130 GMT) until June 27 at 1230 EDT (1630 GMT).

At that hearing, the plaintiffs had intended to ask Dade County Circuit Judge Alan Postman to declare that the settlement pact would not affect the case, which seeks damages from major tobacco companies on behalf of as many 500,000 sick Florida smokers.
The Engle case is set to go to trial on September 8.

Rosenblatt said he did not plan any lawsuit to block the settlement because he did not believe it was intended to stop either the Broin or Engle case, two class-action suits that have already been filed. "In its present form, it 100 percent does not (affect the two cases)," he said.

He also said he had heard nothing from any tobacco company about reaching an out-of-court settlement of the Broin case, now that a settlement was reached that apparently would not affect the class action.
